title: PLY for scans
cards/0/body:
PLY (Polygon File Format) was created at Stanford in the 1990s, the same place that scanned the famous “Stanford bunny”.

First comes a header: how many vertices, what properties they have (x, y, z, color, normal…), how many faces. Then the data itself, as text or in binary.
cards/1/q: Which line says how many vertices there will be?
cards/1/explain: element vertex 120000 means 120 thousand vertices with the listed properties follow.
cards/2/q: This file says element face 0. What does that mean?
cards/2/options/0: There are no faces: it is a point cloud
cards/2/options/2: The faces are in another file
cards/2/explain: PLY happily stores points without faces, which is why scanners love it.
cards/3/body:
You can give vertices any properties: color, normal, scanner confidence, intensity. There may be no faces at all.

That is why PLY is common in photogrammetry, science and robotics.
cards/3/deep: 3D Gaussian Splatting models are usually stored in PLY too: each “point” is a Gaussian with its own properties (scale, rotation, opacity, color coefficients). The format allows this with no extensions, just new property lines.
cards/4/q: A scanner produced millions of colored points. Which of the simple mesh formats fits?
cards/4/explain: STL stores only triangles without color. PLY stores points with any properties.
cards/5/q: What can PLY store? Select all.
cards/5/options/3: Custom properties, such as scanner confidence
cards/5/explain: PLY is a flexible table of vertex and face properties. It has no animation or scene.
cards/6/q: Declare a color property in the PLY header
cards/6/explain: uchar is a byte from 0 to 255, the usual type for color.
cards/7/pairs/0/1: The first line of the file
